title: The verdict that expired
spec: M14 · shelf life, staleness detection, refresh
intro: A cached risk profile answers a $400,000 credit question in 41 milliseconds, with no API call and no hedging. Every fact in it was true on the day it was written, fourteen months ago. Two of them are not true now — and only one of the two has anything watching it.

provenance.source: a narrated UCC credit-decision cache; dates, ages, call volumes and prices are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: This walks M14's milk vs. honey discipline — a per-type shelf life, staleness detected by time or event, and a lazy refresh that pays only where the fact actually spoils.

steps.title: A LOW risk answer in 41 milliseconds
narrative: Credit ops asks whether ACME is clear for a $400,000 revolving line. The profile cache has the debtor, so nothing is fetched: nine stored facts go into the window and the model returns risk: LOW, active_liens: 0, approve. No API call, no latency, no hedge.

Every one of those nine facts was accurate the day it was written — 2025-04-01. That date is in the cache row. It is not in the context window, so the model has no way to weigh it, and nothing downstream asks. The answer is confident because nothing in the pipeline gave it a reason not to be.
steps.youDo: Print the write timestamp beside every cached fact your assembler pulls. A fact whose age never enters the window cannot be reasoned about, by you or by the model.

terminal.text: is ACME LOGISTICS & DISTRIBUTION, L.L.C. clear for a $400,000 revolving line?

steps.title: What happened in the fourteen months
narrative: Query the source of truth instead of the cache and a different debtor appears. On 2025-11-14 — seven months after the profile was written — HARBOR POINT ASSET FUNDING, INC. perfected a $1,200,000 lien over ACME's rolling stock. It has been on the public record ever since.

Line the stored facts up against their shelf lives and the split is exactly the module's fridge. The legal name and the incorporation date are honey: 453 days old and still correct. The registered address is 273 days past its 180-day shelf life. The lien status is 15x past its 30-day shelf life, and it is the one the credit decision turns on.
steps.claudeSays: The cached value and the verified record disagree. Neither of them is corrupt — the cached one is just describing April 2025.

steps.title: The check that catches it
narrative: The fix is not a bigger cache or a shorter global TTL — it is a shelf life per fact type, and a lazy refresh that fires only for the facts that failed it. Two of the four raw facts are stale, so two get re-fetched. The legal name and the incorporation date are never touched.

Time is not the only detector. The get_debtor_history call from the last step is an event — a fresh source contradicting a cached belief — and it invalidates the lien status regardless of its age. Time-based catches the fact that quietly went off; event-based catches the one that went off yesterday, well inside its TTL.
Refreshed, the same question gets the opposite answer: HIGH, one verified active lien, $1,200,000, senior. Two API calls and 380 ms bought a $400,000 decision that is actually about 2026.
steps.youDo: Give every fact type in your store an explicit shelf life — including the ones you decide never expire. An unlisted type is not "no policy"; it is the most dangerous policy, as the next step shows.

terminal.text: stale = [f for f in profile if f.is_stale(now)]

steps.title: The entry nothing was watching
narrative: The table two steps back had four rows. The cache had five entries. risk_verdict is not a fetched fact — it is a conclusion the pipeline derived and then wrote back — so nobody ever added it to the decay table. DECAY.get("risk_verdict") returns None, and None means honey.

So the freshness check runs, reports two stale facts, refreshes them, and passes — while a 453-day-old LOW verdict sits in the same store marked permanently fresh. On the call paths that read the verdict directly instead of re-scoring, nothing fires at all. That is the silent case: a staleness system that is working correctly and still serving April 2025.

The rule that closes it is one line: a derived fact inherits the shortest shelf life of its inputs. The verdict was computed from lien_status, so it expires in 30 days, not never. And decay policy is not free — refreshing everything on every call costs $432 a day at this volume to keep re-fetching a legal name unchanged since 2009. You spend freshness where staleness is expensive, and nowhere else.
steps.claudeSays: The check did not fail. It was never pointed at the entry that mattered, because that entry was written by the pipeline rather than fetched by it.
steps.youDo: Grep your cache for keys that no TTL table mentions. Derived verdicts, scores and summaries are the usual finds — they are exactly the entries a decision reads first.

views.text: Persistence without expiry is not memory, it is a liability with a timestamp. Give every stored key a shelf life, make derived keys inherit the shortest one they depend on, detect staleness by time and by contradicting event, and refresh lazily — because the cost of freshness is a line item you can read, and the cost of staleness is a $400,000 line you cannot.
